sections.heading: The legal rule
Essential ingredients
Statutory illustrations
sections.body:
(a) A commits house-trespass by making a hole through the wall of Z’s house, and putting his hand through the aperture. This is house-breaking
(b) A commits house-trespass by creeping into a ship at a port-hole between decks. This is house-breaking
(c) A commits house-trespass by entering Z’s house through a window. This is house-breaking
(d) A commits house-trespass by entering Z’s house through the door, having opened a door which was fastened. This is house-breaking
(e) A commits house-trespass by entering Z’s house through the door, having lifted a latch by putting a wire through a hole in the door. This is house-breaking
(f) A finds the key of Z’s house door, which Z had lost, and commits house-trespass by entering Z’s house, having opened the door with that key. This is house-breaking
(g) Z is standing in his doorway. A forces a passage by knocking Z down, and commits house-trespass by entering the house. This is house-breaking
(h) Z, the door-keeper of Y, is standing in Y’s doorway. A commits house-trespass by entering the house, having deterred Z from opposing him by threatening to beat him. This is house-breaking

sections.heading: Explanations
sections.body: Explanation.—Any out-house or building occupied with a house, and between which and such house there is an immediate internal communication, is part of the house within the meaning of this section

questionsAndAnswers.answer:
Introduction. BNS s. 330 deals with House-trespass and house-breaking. It sits in Chapter XVII — Of Offences Against Property of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. After 1 July 2024 this is the current-law citation for this offence / definition / punishment.

Meaning. House-trespass and house-breaking. BNS restatement of IPC 443 / 445. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 443 / 445. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.

Legal rule. In student language: BNS s. 330 is the rule on “House-trespass and house-breaking”. The section provides that .(1) Whoever commits house-trespass having taken precautions to conceal such house-trespass from some person who has a right to exclude or eject the trespasser from the building, tent or vessel which is the subject of the trespass, is said to commit lurking house-trespass. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Essential ingredients. An authoritative analysis must list them, not hide them in one paragraph:
1. (1) Whoever commits house-trespass having taken precautions to conceal such house-trespass from some person who has a right to exclude or eject the trespasser from the building, tent or vessel which is the subject of the trespass, is said to commit lurking house-trespass
2. (2) A person is said to commit house-breaking who commits house-trespass if he effects his entrance into the house or any part of it in any of the six ways hereinafter described; or if, being in the house or any part of it for the purpose of committing an offence, or having committed an offence therein, he quits the house or any part of it in any of the following ways, namely:–
3. (a) if he enters or quits through a passage made by himself, or by any abettor of the house-trespass, in order to the committing of the house-trespass;
4. (b) if he enters or quits through any passage not intended by any person, other than himself or an abettor of the offence, for human entrance; or through any passage to which he has obtained access by scaling or climbing over any wall or building;
5. (c) if he enters or quits through any passage which he or any abettor of the house-trespass has opened, in order to the committing of the house-trespass by any means by which that passage was not intended by the occupier of the house to be opened;
6. (d) if he enters or quits by opening any lock in order to the committing of the house-trespass, or in order to the quitting of the house after a house-trespass;
7. (e) if he effects his entrance or departure by using criminal force or committing an assault, or by threatening any person with assault;
8. (f) if he enters or quits by any passage which he knows to have been fastened against such entrance or departure, and to have been unfastened by himself or by an abettor of the house-trespass

Illustrations. The section itself supplies worked examples. In legal analysis, pick one illustration, restate its facts, and show which ingredient it proves. Illustration (a): (a) A commits house-trespass by making a hole through the wall of Z’s house, and putting his hand through the aperture. This is house-breaking

Explanations. Explanation.—Any out-house or building occupied with a house, and between which and such house there is an immediate internal communication, is part of the house within the meaning of this section An explanation is not optional commentary. It is part of the section and must appear in an authoritative brief.

Limitations. Apply only the conditions written in s. 330. Do not import a defence from a different chapter unless the question requires it.

Conclusion. BNS s. 330 is the complete current-law heading for House-trespass and house-breaking. Define, list ingredients, use an illustration, note any explanation or exception, apply, cite. That is a complete statutory structure.

Comprehensive Written Submissions. Deepen the doctrinal synthesis with four foundational layers.

Layer 1 — Place the section in the Chapter. Theft, snatching, extortion, robbery, dacoity, trust, cheating, mischief, trespass.. Show why this heading sits where it sits.

Layer 2 — Work a second statutory illustration. Illustration (b): (b) A commits house-trespass by creeping into a ship at a port-hole between decks. This is house-breaking Contrast it with illustration (a). The legal weight lies in the contrast.

Layer 3 — Analytical comment. Explain a condition, a proviso, or a practical difficulty in applying s. 330. Do not invent case names.



Layer 5 — Application and current-law close. Apply the test to the problem facts in IRAC form (Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion). Close with: “The governing citation on or after 1 July 2024 is BNS s. 330.”

enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 330 defines lurking house-trespass and house-breaking (consolidating former IPC 443-445). Lurking house-trespass involves taking precautions to conceal the trespass from someone who has a right to exclude. House-breaking involves committing house-trespass by entering or quitting through any of six specified ways: (1) through a passage made by the trespasser; (2) through a passage not intended for human entrance (like windows/chimneys); (3) through a passage opened by breaking or unfastening; (4) by unfastening any lock; (5) by using criminal force or committing assault; or (6) entering by any passage fastened against entrance.
examples: Teaching example (Standard application): An individual intentionally commits acts satisfying the statutory formula of house-trespass and house-breaking under Section 330 without lawful authority. The individual is liable under BNS s. 330.

Teaching example (Absence of mens rea / Lawful exception): A person acts in good faith or without the requisite statutory mental element under circumstances recognized by law. The essential ingredients of Section 330 are not satisfied; no penal liability attaches.
distinctions: House-trespass (s. 329) vs House-breaking (s. 330): House-trespass is simple unlawful entry; House-breaking requires entry/exit through one of the six violent or surreptitious statutory methods.
House-breaking vs Burglary: House-breaking is the codified Indian statutory equivalent of common law burglary.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether the accused is liable under BNS s. 330 for conduct relating to house-trespass and house-breaking.
Rule: Under BNS s. 330, liability attaches upon proof of the statutory actus reus accompanied by the requisite mens rea without lawful justification.
Application: The evidence demonstrates that the accused performed the specified act with the required state of mind, satisfying all statutory ingredients of Section 330.
Conclusion: The accused is guilty of an offence under BNS s. 330 and subject to the prescribed punishment.
